scenarios.paper: photosynthesis off ~1.7-2 yr; global cooling up to ~15 degC; recovery ~15-20 yr

list.name: Tanis
list.record: A river bank buried within the first hour or so: sturgeon and paddlefish piled on a sandbar under about 2 m of sediment, impact spherules up to 5 mm in their gill rakers, spherule pits in the mud and spherules caught in amber. Its excavators read it as surges of river water set off by the seismic shaking (a seiche), not a tsunami, which could not have come this far in time. Bone growth in its fish points to spring in the north. The site has been studied mostly by one team, and parts of its interpretation are disputed.
list.refs: DePalma et al. 2019 (PNAS); During et al. 2022 (Nature)

list.name: Hell Creek
list.record: The best-known record of the last dinosaurs: Tyrannosaurus, Triceratops, Edmontosaurus and Ankylosaurus in river and floodplain sands and muds, with mammals, lizards, turtles and birds. At the top lies the boundary clay, centimetres thick, with iridium and shocked quartz under a coal seam; no dinosaur bones are found above it, and more than half the kinds of leaves disappear.

list.name: Raton Basin
list.record: Where the iridium layer was first found in rocks laid down on land: a claystone about a centimetre thick in the coal swamps' beds, with iridium, shocked quartz and spherules. Above it the pollen of flowering plants gives way to fern spores (the 'fern spike'): ferns recolonised the bare ground first.

list.name: Brazos River
list.record: A muddy shelf of the Gulf coast then, tens of metres to a hundred metres deep. At the boundary lies a sandstone bed with torn-up mud clasts, shell debris and impact spherules, read as laid down by the tsunami and the currents the impact set off. Whether it lies exactly at the boundary has been argued.
list.refs: Bourgeois et al. 1988 (Science); Keller et al. 2007

list.name: El Mimbral
list.record: A layered clastic unit up to 3 m thick between the marls of the deep Gulf floor: impact spherules with glass cores at its base, then sandstone, then rippled sands, under an iridium-rich clay. Read as the work of the impact's slumps, turbidity currents and tsunami backwash; Keller and Stinnesbeck argued it built up over a longer time.
list.refs: Smit et al. 1992 (Geology); Stinnesbeck et al. 1993

list.name: Beloc
list.record: Deep Caribbean sea floor then: a bed of impact spherules up to tens of centimetres thick, some still with cores of black and yellow glass whose make-up matches melted Yucatán rock and its evaporites. With shocked quartz and iridium it helped point to Chicxulub as the crater.
list.refs: Sigurdsson et al. 1991 (Nature); Izett 1991; Maurrasse & Sen 1991

list.name: Blake Nose, ODP 1049
list.record: A drill core from the Atlantic slope: a graded bed of green spherules some 10 to 17 cm thick, with shocked quartz and an iridium layer on top; the plankton below it are Cretaceous, those above it Paleocene, with almost nothing surviving across.
list.refs: Norris et al. 1999 (Geology); Klaus et al. 2000

list.name: Demerara Rise, ODP 1259
list.record: Drill cores from a submarine plateau: a spherule bed about a centimetre or two thick, the sudden loss of most plankton above it, and the slow return of life to the open sea in the cores that follow.

list.name: Gubbio
list.record: Pink limestone of the deep Tethys sea floor, broken by a clay about a centimetre thick. Walter and Luis Alvarez's team measured iridium in the clay at some 30 times the level in the limestone and proposed in 1980 that an asteroid had struck and caused the extinction. The foraminifera of the limestone change abruptly across it.

list.name: Stevns Klint
list.record: A 15 km sea cliff in the chalk of a warm northern sea: white Cretaceous chalk, the dark Fish Clay (Fiskeler) a few centimetres thick with fish remains, iridium (about 160 times background, one of the three 1980 sites) and soot from the fires, then Paleocene limestone built by bryozoans. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2014.
list.refs: Alvarez et al. 1980 (Science); Wolbach et al. 1985 (Nature); Surlyk et al. 2013

list.name: Caravaca
list.record: One of the most complete marine sections: a dark boundary clay a few centimetres thick with a reddish basal layer rich in iridium and nickel-rich spinel crystals, where most planktic foraminifera vanish. Its iridium was found the same year as Gubbio's, independently.

list.name: Zumaia
list.record: Flysch cliffs, deep sea floor then, with millions of years in tilted beds: the boundary is a thin dark clay with iridium over the last Cretaceous marls. The same cliffs hold the reference sections of two later Paleocene stages.
list.refs: Smit & ten Kate 1982; Schmitz et al. 2011 (Episodes)

list.name: El Kef
list.record: The official reference section for the start of the Paleogene: the boundary is set at the base of a dark clay with a thin reddish layer rich in iridium, where most planktic foraminifera die out. Oxygen isotopes of fish teeth from here record the warming that followed (about 5 °C), which this viewer's long warm-up follows.
list.refs: Molina et al. 2006 (Episodes); MacLeod et al. 2018 (Science)

list.name: Maastricht
list.record: The town the Maastrichtian, the last age of the Cretaceous, is named after. Its chalk quarries gave up the first mosasaur skull in the 1760s and 1770s, later named Mosasaurus hoffmanni: the sea's top predators, marine reptiles up to some 15 m long, which died out at the boundary.

list.name: Seymour Island
list.record: A shelf sea far south then: the López de Bertodano Formation, rich in ammonites, snails, clams and marine reptiles up to the boundary, which carries iridium and a bed of fish remains just above it. Even this far from the crater the extinction was sudden.
list.refs: Elliot et al. 1994 (Geology); Witts et al. 2016 (Nat. Commun.)

list.name: Woodside Creek
list.record: Limestone of the open southern ocean, among the farthest boundary sites from the crater: the third of the 1980 iridium sites, with a thin dark clay that also holds soot.
list.refs: Alvarez et al. 1980 (Science); Wolbach et al. 1985 (Nature)

list.name: Lameta beds
list.record: Nesting grounds of the last dinosaurs of India: titanosaur eggs and bones in the Lameta beds, beneath and between the first lavas of the Deccan Traps. The Deccan eruptions were flooding India with lava before and after the impact; how much they added to the extinction is still argued.
list.refs: Mohabey 1996; Schoene et al. 2019 (Science); Sprain et al. 2019 (Science)
